name: Tantra as a movement across the traditions (Tantraśāstra; the Mantramārga / Mantranaya current)

tradition.text: Each family holds its tantras to be beginningless revelation: the Śaiva scriptures spoken from the five faces of Sadāśiva; the Pāñcarātra by Nārāyaṇa; the Buddhist tantras by the Buddha as Vajradhara (the Kālacakra at Dhānyakaṭaka); Jain vidyās from the lost Vidyānupravāda Pūrva.

scholarly.text: Earliest surviving Śaiva tantric scripture (Niśvāsa) c. 5th–7th c. CE; Buddhist Kriyā and Yoga tantras 6th–8th c.; Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha and Buddhist Yoginī tantras 8th–10th c.; Kālacakra early 11th c.; Jain mantra-kalpas 10th–11th c.; later Bengal and Kerala digests 14th–17th c.

transmissions_received.what: the vocabulary and forms of fire-offering (homa), consecration (dīkṣā, abhiṣeka) and mantra
the Śaiva ascetic heritage (ash, skull, cremation ground, five brahma-mantras)
dhāraṇī, bodhicitta and emptiness as the ground of the Buddhist Mantranaya

transmissions_given.what: kuṇḍalinī, the centres, bindu and the mudrās (through Kaula and Buddhist tantric yoga)
tantric pūjā, nyāsa and mantra taken into the later Purāṇas
the vocabulary of sahaja, śūnya, the tenth door and the reversed current, through the Nāths and the siddhas' songs
sahaja, the body as the seat of the divine couple, coded speech
tantric cycles and Great Perfection vocabulary shared with Buddhism

distinctive_positions: Liberation and power (mukti and bhukti/siddhi) are both legitimate aims of practice; the aspirant chooses between them or seeks both (Śaiva sādhaka and mumukṣu; Buddhist ordinary and supreme siddhi; the Kaula 'enjoyment becomes yoga').
Practice begins with initiation (dīkṣā, abhiṣeka) by a qualified guru into a lineage and a mantra; without it the teaching is not to be practised.
Mantra is the deity in sound: the mantra is the deity's body, and repetition with the correct form, seed syllables and nyāsa makes the deity present.
One worships the deity by becoming the deity ('only a god may worship a god'; Buddhist divine pride; the Pāñcarātra sādhaka's identification with Viṣṇu).
The body is a maṇḍala: channels, centres, seats (pīṭha) and letters are installed or discovered in it, and the outer sacred geography is mapped onto it.
The guru is the deity present in human form; the teaching is secret and given only to the qualified.
Purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the placing of mantras (nyāsa) precede worship; the maṇḍala or yantra is the deity's palace and body.
In the Kaula and Yoginī strata, transgressive substances and acts are used or — more commonly in the surviving traditions — reinterpreted as inner yoga; each family records its own warnings.
Each family places its tantras above the Veda or the sūtras (as a higher or more rapid revelation) while usually denying that they contradict them.
The movement is not one tradition: its Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain forms keep their own ultimate, ethics and goal, and each rejects the others' final view.
summary: An umbrella entry, owned by U49, for tantra as a movement that runs across families rather than a single lineage: the Śaiva Mantramārga (Siddhānta, Bhairava and Kaula scriptures), the Śākta traditions (Śrīvidyā, Kālīkula, Kubjikā), the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra, the Buddhist Mantranaya/Vajrayāna and the Jain mantra-kalpas (Padmāvatī, Jvālāmālinī). They share a ritual and yogic grammar — initiation, mantra, maṇḍala and yantra, nyāsa and bhūtaśuddhi, deity identification, the subtle body, the guru as deity, secrecy, and the twin goals of power and liberation — while each keeps its own view of the ultimate. Its links are recorded as borrowings (brw:*) with typed evidence.
notes: Classificatory umbrella (merge.py lists it among UMBRELLAS): it is not an independent root for convergence counts. sub_lineages lists the family lineages that belong to the movement; their own 'parent' fields are not changed by this unit.
